title: The Prince and Me
full_review:
A career-conscious undergrad falls for a charming exchange student only to discover he is actually European royalty in the breezy but bland storybook romance, "The Prince & Me" (Paramount).

Julia Stiles stars as Paige Morgan, a fiercely focused pre-med candidate at the University of Wisconsin. Raised on a rural dairy farm, Paige's workaholic ways have set her on the yellow-brick road to creating the life she's always wanted. After graduation she plans to study medicine at Johns Hopkins University and then work as a doctor in the Third World.

Across the Atlantic, Edvard's (Luke Mably) life has also been mapped out. When it is his time he will ascend the throne of Denmark and take his place in the world's longest continuous monarchy.

In the meantime, the playboy crown prince is much more concerned about partying with Eurotrash models and drag-racing his Lamborghini through the streets of Copenhagen than with matters of state -- much to the delight of the Danish tabloids. Prompted by a sleazy video of loose American college coeds, he decides to take a detour from his destiny and enroll incognito -- where else -- at the University of Wisconsin.

Edvard's long-suffering parents, the king and queen (James Fox and Miranda Richardson) reluctantly indulge their spoiled scion, provided that Soren (Ben Miller), the prince's loyal equerry (royal speak for baby sitter) accompanies him.

On his first night on campus, "Eddie," as he introduces himself, proves a royal pain when he makes a move on Paige in the student pub where she works.

Swiping its basic premise from "Roman Holiday" (1953), this far inferior narrative unfolds with formulaic predictability as romance blossoms. Despite their blueblood/blue-collar differences, Paige opens herself to love and Eddie realizes that, for the first time in his life, someone likes him for who he is rather than who he is destined to become. Paige invites Eddie home to the farm for Thanksgiving, where he endears himself to her hardworking folks by winning a local souped-up lawn-mower race.

But when the European paparazzi finally track down their royal quarry, Eddie's true identity is revealed. Feeling betrayed, Paige storms off and Eddie returns home to be with his ailing father. Paige puts med school on hold and hops a flight to Denmark in hopes of a fairy-tale ending. But once there, she learns the steep price of living happily ever after.

To quote a slightly better tale about a conflicted young prince, "There is something rotten in Denmark," namely, this cliche-riddled film, which at almost two hours in length is far too long -- and feels it.

For the optimist, Stiles shines, proving that, even amid such mediocrity, one can always see the glass slipper half full. Mably cuts a charming Prince Charming, but his transformation from silver-spoon spoiled brat to greasy-spoon nice guy is a bit unconvincing. Miller provides much comic relief as Eddie�s manservant.

On the one hand, "The Prince & Me" can be seen as a sweet modern fairy tale about the risks and rewards of love. However, as directed by Martha Coolidge, the argument can also be made that the film, in fact, retools the traditional fairy-tale formula, giving it a postmodern feminist twist.

By redefining the criteria of what constitutes "happily ever after," the movie elevates personal fulfillment (a good thing in itself) to the same level of desirability enjoyed by true love in classic fairy tales. It's not that the script paints romance as a negative, but that compromise plays such a small part in the final tally. In this film, Cinderella wants to keep her options open. One could say Princess Paige wants to have her tiara and wear it too!

Due to some crude language and humor, mild sexual situations, and a casual attitude toward student drinking, the USCCB Office for Film & Broadcasting classification is A-III -- adults. The Motion Picture Association of America rating is PG-- parental guidance suggested.
